claims.claim: UK GDPR Article 35(9): where appropriate, the controller shall seek the views of data subjects or their representatives on the intended processing.

Since 6 April 2020, a request for information and consultation arrangements under the ICE Regulations 2004 needs 2% of employees, at least 15 and at most 2,500, in an undertaking with 50 or more employees. The Regulations cover Great Britain.
Section 87(1) no. 6 BetrVG gives German works councils co-determination over the introduction and use of technical devices intended to monitor employees' behaviour or performance.
The Federal Labour Court reads section 87(1) no. 6 widely: a device objectively able to monitor is enough.

concept_html:
A people analytics tool can be lawful under UK GDPR and still stall at go-live, because nobody consulted the people it watches. Consultation duties come from employment law, not data protection law, and they differ by country.

United Kingdom. There is no general works council duty. Three sources still apply:

  • The ICO's monitoring workers guidance (October 2023) expects you to consult workers and their representatives before monitoring, unless there is a good reason not to.
  • UK GDPR Article 35(9) asks you, where appropriate, to seek the views of data subjects or their representatives in a DPIA.
  • Recognised trade unions, collective agreements, or an agreement under the Information and Consultation of Employees Regulations 2004 can set formal duties. In Great Britain, since 6 April 2020, 2% of employees, at least 15, can request such an agreement in a firm of 50 or more.

EU countries go further. A few examples:

  • Germany: the works council has a co-determination right over technical systems designed to monitor behaviour or performance. Courts read "designed" as "able", so most HR software is in scope.
  • France: the works council (CSE) must be consulted before new technology goes live. Courts have suspended AI tools deployed early.
  • Netherlands: the works council has a consent right over personnel monitoring systems and rules on employee data.

The EU AI Act adds a duty for employers to inform workers' representatives before using a high-risk AI system, which includes most hiring and promotion tools. The 2026 amendments moved those high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027. National duties apply now.

Treat this as a map, not advice. Ask the employment lawyers in each country before go-live.

lines: CONSULTATION_RULES = {
"DE": {"body": "works council", "triggers": {"monitoring", "high_risk_ai"}},
"FR": {"body": "CSE", "triggers": {"new_technology", "monitoring", "high_risk_ai"}},
"UK": {"body": "workers and representatives", "triggers": {"monitoring"}},
}
def consult_before_go_live(sites: list[str], features: set[str]) -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
"""Each site's body to consult, from rules the employment lawyers maintain."""
plan = []
for country in sorted(set(sites)):
rule = CONSULTATION_RULES.get(country)
if rule is None:
raise ValueError(f"no consultation rule for {country}: ask the lawyers")
if rule["triggers"] & features:
plan.append((country, rule["body"]))
return plan

notes.html: The rules are data the lawyers own. In production they load from a versioned file.
An unknown country stops the plan. Silence would read as no duty.
What the tool does decides the duty, not the country alone.

example.takeaway_html: Consultation turns on what the tool does and where the people are. Keep the rules as data the lawyers own, and fail loudly on a country nobody has assessed.

exercises.primer:
`&` on two sets gives the items in both. An empty set is falsy:

```python
{"red", "blue"} & {"blue", "green"}   # {"blue"}
bool({"red"} & {"green"})             # False
```

`dict.get(key)` returns `None` for a missing key instead of raising: `{"a": 1}.get("b")` is `None`.

`sorted(set(items))` drops repeats and sorts: `sorted(set(["b", "a", "b"]))` is `["a", "b"]`.

Write `consult_before_go_live(sites: list[str], features: set[str], rules: dict[str, dict]) -> list[tuple[str, str]]`.

`sites` lists the country codes where affected employees work, possibly with repeats. `features` names what the tool does, such as `"monitoring"`. `rules` maps a country code to `{"body": str, "triggers": set[str]}`.

Return `(country, body)` for each distinct country whose triggers share at least one feature with the tool, sorted by country. Raise `ValueError` for a country that has no rule.

Write consult_before_go_live(sites: list[str], features: set[str], rules: dict[str, dict]) -> list[tuple[str, str]].

sites lists the country codes where affected employees work, possibly with repeats. features names what the tool does, such as "monitoring". rules maps a country code to {"body": str, "triggers": set[str]}.

Return (country, body) for each distinct country whose triggers share at least one feature with the tool, sorted by country. Raise ValueError for a country that has no rule.
exercises.solution:
def consult_before_go_live(
    sites: list[str], features: set[str], rules: dict[str, dict]
) -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
    """The body to consult in each country before go-live.

    Args:
        sites: Country codes where affected employees work. Repeats are allowed.
        features: What the tool does, such as "monitoring".
        rules: Country code to {"body": str, "triggers": set[str]}.

    Returns:
        (country, body) for each distinct country the tool triggers, sorted by country.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If a country has no rule.
    """
    plan: list[tuple[str, str]] = []
    for country in sorted(set(sites)):
        rule = rules.get(country)
        if rule is None:
            raise ValueError(f"no consultation rule for {country}")
        if rule["triggers"] & features:
            plan.append((country, rule["body"]))
    return plan

title: Works councils and consultation before people analytics or AI
why_html: A firm rolled out an attrition-risk model to managers in France and Germany on the same day as the UK. In Germany, the works council had not agreed to it. In France, the works council had not given its opinion. Both sites switched the tool off within weeks. The UK pilot, where the team had consulted staff and recorded their views in the DPIA, kept running.
